chapter: Lover Man and the postwar years
title: The risque lyric of "Lover Man"
summary: The lyrics were thought too earthy; Walter Bishop said to keep them; Billie's recording gave carte blanche.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: And of course, at that time... To go on with my story... I had asked Walter to do the lyric on "Lover Man" because it... "I go to bed with a prayer" and all that; you know, in those days it was a no-no. "You'll make love to me" -- it was very earthy in those days.
I thought you said somebody called Davis did these lyrics.
Yeah. But they claimed they got complaints about...

And "I go to bed with prayers you'll make love to me." In those days the only one who could sing it and get away with it would be Billie Holiday. But look, when you get a gay imitator, you know he had to get away with

it -- he was the only one there. So he really broke the ice. So Walter said, "No man, leave the lyric like that. No! Leave it like that." And Walter is that way, you know. And that way, the public began to accept, you know, "Love-er man..." -- that got it, you know. And then, those lurid lyrics and sexy lyrics at that time, that means that singers... Well, when Billie put it out, naturally with her following, that gave it the carte blanche.

Well, the rest is history, you know, because singers sing it, instrumentalists liked it... Well, like "How High The Moon" or "Body and Soul" will always be around; so "Lover Man" looks like it will always be around.

Now, it was hard getting that baby off the ground, because I remember (?) was telling me, "Why don't you make a polka out of it?" "Oh, this is... Do this, do that, do that." I couldn't get nobody up with it, you know!
